titre: The Captain No One Could Read
accroche: James Cook dies on a Hawaiian beach on February 14, 1779. Since 1992, two anthropologists have argued over whether he was taken for a god.
contenu_vulgarise:
On January 17, 1779, Captain James Cook's two ships entered Kealakekua Bay, on the coast of Hawaiʻi. The inhabitants welcomed them with unusual pomp: thousands of people, processions, priests who seemed to treat Cook as a guest of a very particular rank. This arrival coincided with the Makahiki, the New Year festival devoted to Lono, a god associated with fertility and rain. Cook left on February 4. A storm damaged one of the Resolution's masts, forcing the expedition to return on the 11th. Three days later, on February 14, 1779, a clash on the beach over a stolen boat turned into a fight: Cook was killed.

## A God, or a Chiefly Title?

In 1985, in Islands of History, the anthropologist Marshall Sahlins argued that Hawaiians identified Cook with the god Lono because his arrival coincided with the Makahiki calendar. His forced return, after Lono's ritual departure, would have collided head-on with the cosmological cycle then giving way to the war god, Kū. For Sahlins, Cook's death is therefore not a raw accident, but the product of a clash between two calendars, Hawaiian and naval, that could only collide that year.

In 1992, in The Apotheosis of Captain Cook, the anthropologist Gananath Obeyesekere disputed this account point by point. Drawing on the logbooks of Cook's officers, he argued that Hawaiians treated Cook as a chief of high rank, a political title, not as a deity. He claimed the idea of a Cook taken for a god originated less in Hawaiʻi than in England, in the imagination of Europeans themselves, who wanted to see in this welcome proof of their own superiority. The Hawaiians, in his view, acted out of ordinary political calculation, not mythological misunderstanding.

## A Debate That Never Closes

Sahlins replied in 1995 in How “Natives” Think: About Captain Cook, For Example, taking up Obeyesekere's arguments one by one. The exchange continued without either side winning general agreement: to this day, specialists remain divided on whether Hawaiians saw Cook as a deity.

What makes the quarrel instructive goes beyond Cook himself: at its core lies how to understand the rationality of Indigenous peoples. Obeyesekere held that Hawaiians thought essentially like Westerners, and worried that arguing otherwise would make them look “irrational” and “uncivilized.” Sahlins argued the opposite: that each culture may have its own rationality, and that assuming a single reason for all is a form of Eurocentrism.

repere.texte: Cook's Resolution left Kealakekua Bay on February 4, 1779, was forced back by a storm that damaged a mast on the 11th, and Cook died there three days later, on February 14.

carte.punch: Two anthropologists argued for years over whether Hawaiʻi had taken an English captain for a god.
carte.idee: James Cook dies in Hawaiʻi on February 14, 1779. For Sahlins (1985), Hawaiians identified him with the god Lono according to their ritual calendar. For Obeyesekere (1992), this account is a European myth: Hawaiians would have treated him as a chief, out of political calculation.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Precise dates of Cook's stay at Kealakekua, and the state of scholarly opinion, divided on whether Hawaiians saw Cook as a deity.

quiz.question: Why, according to Marshall Sahlins, did Cook's forced return to Kealakekua Bay on February 11, 1779, have such grave consequences?
choix: Because Cook's crew had stolen food intended for Hawaiian priests
Because it violated the ritual calendar of the Makahiki, in which the god Lono must give way to the war god Kū
Because Cook had refused to take part in the Makahiki ceremonies in January
Because the Hawaiians had already decided to kill him during his first visit, in January
quiz.explication: For Sahlins, Cook's arrival coincided with the season of the god Lono during the Makahiki; his return after that god's ritual departure would have collided with the cosmological cycle then giving way to Kū, the war god, which would explain the turn toward confrontation. Obeyesekere would dispute this reading precisely.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Gananath Obeyesekere argue in The Apotheosis of Captain Cook (1992)?
choix: That Cook proclaimed himself a god to the Hawaiians as soon as he arrived
That the Hawaiians never met Cook before the battle of February 14
That Hawaiians treated Cook as a chief of high rank, out of political calculation, not as a deity
That the logbooks of Cook's officers were destroyed before ever being studied
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Obeyesekere draws on the logbooks of Cook's officers to argue that Hawaiians granted him a chiefly title, an ordinary political gesture, and that the story of his deification is a myth forged in Europe rather than a Hawaiian belief.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does Marshall Sahlins respond to Obeyesekere's critique, in 1995?
choix: He refuses to comment publicly on Obeyesekere's book
He comes around to Obeyesekere's thesis in a new edition of his own book
He has Obeyesekere's book withdrawn from sale through legal action
He publishes How Natives Think: About Captain Cook, For Example, taking up Obeyesekere's arguments one by one
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Sahlins responds directly with an entire book, How Natives Think, devoted to dismantling point by point the arguments Obeyesekere had advanced three years earlier.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Beyond the case of Cook, what is the underlying disagreement between Sahlins and Obeyesekere?
choix: How to understand the rationality of Indigenous peoples: thinking like Westerners for one, a rationality specific to each culture for the other
Both accuse each other of falsifying the dates of their research trips to Hawaiʻi
Both admit they never read the expedition's original logbooks
Neither ever set foot in Hawaiʻi before writing his book
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Obeyesekere holds that Indigenous peoples think essentially like Westerners and worries that arguing otherwise would make them look “irrational”; Sahlins argues that each culture may have its own rationality and calls the idea of a single reason Eurocentrism.
